article_title: Vocabulary Improvement Program for English Language Learners and Their Classmates (VIP) (English Language Learners)
citation: Vocabulary Improvement Program for English Language Learners and Their Classmates. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.brookespublishing.com/store/books/lively-6342/index.htm
title: Weekly vocabulary cycle: native-language preview, English introduction, small-group word tasks, and word-analysis Friday
description: VIP organizes instruction as a repeating weekly cycle around a weekly reading assignment. "On Mondays English language learner students are given the weekly reading assignment in their native language to preview before it is introduced in English on the following day." Tuesdays bring whole-group lessons defining target vocabulary; Wednesdays use heterogeneous language groups for two cloze activities; Thursdays use small groups for word association, synonym/antonym, and semantic feature analysis; Fridays cover root-word analysis and multiple meanings of words.
requirements: Bilingual capacity or materials to provide the native-language (Spanish) preview on Monday
Heterogeneous grouping based on English language proficiency for mid-week activities
constraints: Evaluated in grades 4-6 with Spanish-speaking English language learners in bilingual and mainstream classrooms
target_learning_goals: depth of vocabulary knowledge
word meaning, morphology, and multiple meanings
examples: In the study, three lessons observed during weeks 4, 9, and 13 revealed six of nine intervention teachers implemented more than 70% of key lesson elements
key_sources: Vocabulary Improvement Program for English Language Learners and Their Classmates. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.brookespublishing.com/store/books/lively-6342/index.htm

article_title: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Build in visual organizers that learners can manipulate to help adult learners visualize and organize information
description: The brief's second principle recommends visual or graphic organizers as mental scaffolding that mimics how the brain records and organizes information. The brief says visual organizers "replicate this map for learners, helping them understand and therefore strengthen the patterns being formed between old and new information," supporting four functions: clarifying thoughts, organizing and analyzing information, integrating new knowledge, and thinking critically. Although widespread in K-12, such tools are used by few adult learning products.
requirements: Tools should let learners create, manipulate, and change organizers as their learning develops
Organizers should connect learners' prior experience to new content
constraints: Visual organizers are used by few, if any, adult learning products, so designers must adapt K-12 tools
target_learning_goals: organizing and analyzing information
integrating new knowledge
critical thinking
examples: K-12 visual tools such as Inspiration let learners create maps and flow charts, use templates or their own organizers, and manipulate them as learning deepens
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0b18a16a-2f1d-400b-9fed-df5675ba40cf

article_title: Unintended Impact: How the Verizon Innovative Learning Schools Program Affected Its Educators' Job Satisfaction and Career Trajectories
citation: Chelimo, S., Cortez, C., Jackson, J., & Weaver, D. (2024, May). Unintended Impact: How the Verizon Innovative Learning Schools Program Affected Its Educators' Job Satisfaction and Career Trajectories. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/212
title: Three standout reasons for increased job satisfaction: technology access and use, student engagement, and work-life balance
description: Interviews of teachers and coaches did not uncover a single distinct reason for increased job satisfaction but a multiplicity, of which three stood out: the availability and effective use of technology, increased student engagement leading to less teacher stress, and better work-life balance from digital convenience. The report presents these as recurring themes across the six districts rather than tested factors, illustrated with teacher and coach testimonies about engagement, joy, and time management.
requirements: Program-supported devices and connectivity plus coaching that helps teachers use technology effectively
constraints: Derived from interviews and focus groups in six districts; the report notes no distinct single reason was found
target_learning_goals: teacher retention and job satisfaction
student engagement through technology
examples: A Broward teacher reported spending less time working out of school hours because being digitally connected let her get more done in school

article_title: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: SPICE Family Literacy Program, Central Maine
citation: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: SPICE. (2012). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Use a virtual world to provide real community and human connection as an antidote to rural isolation in adult education
description: The article argues that a virtual world can supply the community and human support that adult learners need and that traditional distance education lacks. Because "every avatar has a real person behind it," learners interact with teachers and peers in real time, and the article claims the multiple digital channels for human support can provide more learner-educator connections than face-to-face programs. SPICE used this to address the loneliness its adult learners reported in a 2008 state audit.
requirements: Teachers trained to interact with every avatar so each learner experiences human connection
Understanding what your learners need before adopting the approach
constraints: Hughes notes family literacy programs in less rural areas might not have the same success with a virtual world if their learners have a physical place to meet
target_learning_goals: community building, persistence, and confidence in adult and family literacy education
examples: SPICE educators went to learners' homes across RSU 3's 440 square miles before building the virtual Center, and learners report no longer feeling isolated
key_sources: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: SPICE. (2012). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org

article_title: Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Formative Assessment and Agency as Drivers of Instructional Transformation
citation: Center on School Turnaround at WestEd. (2018). Thought Leadership Forum brief: Formative assessment and agency as drivers of instructional transformation. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://centeronschoolturnaround.org
title: VITAL (Visibly Improve Teaching and Learning) professional learning service
description: VITAL is a WestEd service "to build teachers' capacity to engage in effective collaboration focused on teacher and student learning." It provides tools and processes establishing a professional teaching/learning cycle in four phases: prepare for inquiry, engage in a teaching-and-learning cycle, study impact on student and teacher learning, and take action to share findings. In phase 2, teachers plan lessons, seek peer feedback, teach and observe lessons (e.g., through video), analyze student work, and offer collaborative feedback.
requirements: Collaborative settings in which teachers make their practice visible, supported by structures and tools for self-reflection, structured and rigorous dialogue, and formative peer feedback
target_learning_goals: Improving instructional practice through collaborative inquiry and formative peer feedback
examples: In phase 2 of the VITAL cycle, individual teachers plan a lesson, seek peer feedback, teach and observe others' lessons, analyze student work, and offer feedback in collaborative settings

article_title: Collaborative Making of a Boundary Object for Classifying Generative AI Learning Activities
citation: Dohn, N. B., Markauskaite, L., Huber, E., Wardak, D., Yang, H., Zeivots, S., Casey, A., van Diggele, C., Dohn, N. B., Mannix, K., Mantai, L., Pressick-Kilborn, K., Spence, N., Vallis, C., & Wilson, S. (2026). Collaborative Making of a Boundary Object for Classifying Generative AI Learning Activities. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00671-3
title: Develop taxonomies iteratively through visible, dialogic testing against concrete examples
description: Following Bowker and Star's recommendation to enhance classification flexibility by "rendering the process of categorisation visible and classificatory voices retrievable," the article developed its taxonomy iteratively through a postdigital dialogue in which the initial prototype was tested and reconfigured against concrete examples. The dialogue involved a face-to-face workshop with four groups testing the taxonomy against shared examples, followed by written dialogue integrating elaborations and restructurings. This approach responds to the field's dynamicity and encourages readers' creative and flexible uses of the taxonomy.
requirements: Multiple voices with diverse backgrounds and institutional roles
Concrete examples for testing the taxonomy
A follow-up written dialogue to integrate group suggestions
constraints: The three design requirements for classifications (comparability, visibility, control) trade off against each other due to the wildness and complexity of what is represented
target_learning_goals: systematising emerging pedagogical practices
developing shared terminology for new educational phenomena
examples: The first author produced an initial prototype and presented it at a workshop where four groups tested it against new examples, identifying elaborations and restructurings

article_title: Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs
citation: Jacob Levine, Miguel Aenlle, Craig Zilles, Matthew West, and Mariana Silva. (2026). Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19043
title: Recurring failure modes of vision-LLM grading of handwritten math: blurry images, rotated text, hallucinated text, missing solution elements, and erroneous mathematical reasoning
description: The article's qualitative analysis of discrepant submissions identifies several recurring failure modes: transcription errors due to blurry submissions, transcription errors due to rotated text, hallucinated text, correctness assigned despite missing solution elements, and erroneous mathematical reasoning. The authors note LLMs "produced substantially more accurate transcripts for well-captured images, whereas blurred submissions were sometimes ambiguous even to course staff." Hallucinated text was most common with blurry or rotated images, suggesting higher-quality inputs may reduce this risk.
requirements: Well-captured, clear, well-organized submissions for reliable transcription
constraints: Correctness assigned despite missing solution elements may be an inherent LLM limitation
Penalization of rotated images may be impractical in high-stakes exams
target_learners: university STEM students submitting handwritten mathematical work
target_learning_goals: accurate automated rubric-based grading of handwritten multi-step solutions
examples: In Course 1, blurriness often resulted from students photographing solutions written on a tablet; the team added direct screenshot uploads supporting webcam capture, mobile photos, or direct file upload

article_title: Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition
citation: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096
title: Make algorithmic memory predictions visible to build learner metacognition and trust
description: Memdora displays each card's current FSRS-6 retention percentage during review and per-card retention estimates alongside next review dates in the deck browser, "enabling learners to identify their weakest cards at a glance". The design principle is that "transparency builds metacognition: making algorithmic memory predictions visible promotes learner trust and self-regulation", responding to SmartFlash's finding that transparency in AI educational systems is essential for learner acceptance.
requirements: A scheduling algorithm that computes per-card retention estimates, displayed during review and in the deck browser
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness of one's own memory state
examples: Every card displays the current retention percentage computed by FSRS-6 in the top-right corner during review

article_title: When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals?
citation: Zhengxu Li, Junling Wang, and April Yi Wang. (2026). When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals? arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10672
title: Visual4Math: a web-based research prototype instantiating three control-timing paradigms for mathematics visual authoring
description: The authors "developed a web-based research prototype that instantiates three interaction conditions within the same domain", all supporting creation of visuals for primary mathematics word problems while differing in when teachers intervene. Pre-gen uses a conversational interface routing classified intents; mid-gen generates an editable JSON layout of bounding boxes before rendering; post-gen uses Math2Visual to render problems as editable SVG elements on a canvas. The prototype is released at https://github.com/ViktorLee426/Visual4Math with supplementary materials on OSF.
requirements: The system relies on multimodal large language models (GPT-5 for text understanding, GPT-image-1.5 for image generation) and a FastAPI backend with a React frontend.
constraints: The prototype was evaluated only in single-session, remote think-aloud use with standardized arithmetic problems from a curated dataset of 173 textbook-derived examples.
target_learning_goals: authoring visuals for arithmetic word problems covering addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division
examples: In the workflow example, the same cupcake multiplication problem was authored under all three paradigms, with the teacher correcting object counts via region-level prompting, layout editing, or direct SVG manipulation.
key_sources: Zhengxu Li, Junling Wang, and April Yi Wang. (2026). When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals? arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10672

article_title: Securing the Sandbox: A Rootless Containerized Framework for Process-Oriented Monitoring in Computer Graphics Education
citation: Germán Arroyo, Luis López, and Juan Carlos Torres. (2026). Securing the Sandbox: A Rootless Containerized Framework for Process-Oriented Monitoring in Computer Graphics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05929
title: VISMATIC: a secured, low-cost JupyterHub sandbox for process-oriented monitoring in Computer Graphics education
description: VISMATIC is a defense-in-depth framework pairing a JupyterHub execution environment with rootless Podman containerization, loop-device ext4 storage quotas, an Apache2 SSL reverse proxy, and Raspberry Pi hardware. It intercepts explicit HTTP API requests—file modifications, kernel executions, and terminal operations—rather than passive heartbeats, so instructors can "analyze macro-level interaction rhythms and immediately flag the sudden 'copy-paste' injections characteristic of off-platform generative AI usage." Student accounts are provisioned via CSV-based initialization with randomized credentials and animal-themed pseudonyms, keeping behavioral logs cryptographically separated from academic records.
requirements: A closed-source, server-side-only Computer Graphics library so students must remain connected to the platform to complete activities
Centralized JupyterHub orchestration with PAM-based isolated system accounts and an Apache2 reverse proxy with mandatory SSL encryption
constraints: The authors state that no system can achieve absolute security; the contribution is a defense-in-depth mitigation, not a guarantee
The approach cannot extract sub-second keystroke patterns, only macro-level interactions
target_learners: undergraduate and master's Computer Graphics students
target_learning_goals: authentic iterative programming practice
mathematical foundations of computer graphics such as geometric transformations, lighting models, and rendering pipelines
examples: Deployed on a Raspberry Pi 5 with each student session capped at 1.5 CPU cores and 0.5 GB RAM, evaluated with a pilot cohort of 19 active students
key_sources: Germán Arroyo, Luis López, and Juan Carlos Torres. (2026). Securing the Sandbox: A Rootless Containerized Framework for Process-Oriented Monitoring in Computer Graphics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05929

article_title: Vibe Compiler: A Research-Logic Synthesis Tool That Runs without Prompt Engineering -Toward Enhancing Metacognition for Sustaining Agency in the Age of Generative AI-
citation: Riichiro Mizoguchi, Tomoki Aburatani, Kento Koike, Machi Shimmei. (2026). Vibe Compiler: A Research-Logic Synthesis Tool That Runs without Prompt Engineering —Toward Enhancing Metacognition for Sustaining Agency in the Age of Generative AI—. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05545
title: Vibe Compiler: a research-logic compiler that turns Vibes into research logic via a 16-parameter paper ontology
description: Vibe Compiler is a prototype research-logic compiler, built on NotebookLM and Gemini, that helps researchers turn vague intuitions (Vibes) into coherent research logic. It "treats compilation failures as signs that logical components are missing" and, rather than filling gaps autonomously, "returns reflective questions that prompt researchers to develop the missing reasoning themselves." It puts the 16 parameters of a paper ontology to work as a type system, with a dialogue design and user interface equipped with Null checks, consistency checks, probing triggers, and an acceptance path for reverse Analysis.
requirements: Seven kinds of content-oriented materials must be fed in; the ontology runs as unformalized prose documents written for human readers
Objective structural indicators must be computed with accuracy acceptable in practice
constraints: The Oracle premise can break down as difficulty rises, which the design treats as an occasion for evaluation
Quantitative effects on evaluative judgment (RQ2, RQ3, RQ5) are formulated but not yet verified
target_learning_goals: Articulating missing logical components in research plans
Maintaining epistemic agency when using generative AI
examples: The prototype executed the type check against the paper ontology and built the logical structure of the position paper itself, with execution logs as support

article_title: Artificial Intelligence in Science Learning within the Framework of Situated Learning Theory: A Qualitative Investigation of Teachers' Perspectives
citation: Li, S. (2025). Artificial Intelligence in Science Learning within the Framework of Situated Learning Theory: A Qualitative Investigation of Teachers' Perspectives. Creative Education, 16, 1858-1882. https://doi.org/10.4236/ce.2025.1611114
title: Complementary learning ecosystem combining virtual labs and simulations with generative AI assistants
description: Teachers in this study employed two primary categories of AI tools in science instruction: virtual labs and simulations, which emphasize visualization and hands-on exploration of phenomena in risk-free environments, and generative AI applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, KIMI, and Deepseek, which provide personalized guidance and step-by-step problem-solving support. Rather than adopting tools in isolation, teachers strategically combined them to align with lesson goals. As one teacher summarized, generative AI stimulates thinking while virtual labs emphasize hands-on practice, creating a complementary ecosystem in which cognitive reasoning and experiential exploration mutually reinforce one another.
requirements: Teachers select and combine tool types in accordance with their pedagogical objectives and the specific goals and contexts of their science lessons.
constraints: The pattern is described from teachers of physics, chemistry, mathematics, and general science in Chinese K-12 settings; the article does not claim generalization beyond these contexts.
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of abstract scientific phenomena
Inquiry and experimental design skills
Self-directed learning
examples: Virtual physics laboratories simulating particle motion in magnetic fields with adjustable parameters, alongside AI tutoring systems analyzing learning data to deliver tailored feedback.

article_title: ADHD Subtype Differences in Reinforcement Sensitivity and Visuospatial Working Memory
citation: Dovis, S., Van der Oord, S., Wiers, R.W., & Prins, P.J.M. (2015). ADHD subtype differences in reinforcement sensitivity and visuospatial working memory. Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology, 44(5), 859-874. https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2014.895940
title: Dual-component model of visuospatial working memory: short-term memory and central executive
description: The article adopts a model in which visuospatial working memory "is composed of short-term memory (STM) and a central executive (CE)". It uses this decomposition to locate subtype-specific deficits: in ADHD-C both components seem impaired, whereas in ADHD-I only the CE appears impaired while STM is intact. The model also allows motivational impairments to be traced to their effects on the separate WM components. This componential framing organizes the study's experimental comparisons of STM, CE and WM performance across subtypes and reinforcement conditions.
requirements: Tasks must separately index STM and CE components of visuospatial working memory for the decomposition to be tested.
constraints: The article notes that in children with ADHD-C the components only "seem impaired", and no prior studies had investigated these WM components in children with ADHD-I.
target_learning_goals: visuospatial working memory performance
examples: The study examined effects of standard and high reinforcement on visuospatial WM-, STM-, and CE performance across the two ADHD subtypes and controls.

article_title: Limited knowledge of fraction representations differentiates middle school students with mathematics learning disability (dyscalculia) versus low mathematics achievement
citation: Mazzocco, M. M. M., Myers, G. F., Lewis, K. E., Hanich, L. B., & Murphy, M. M. (2013). Limited knowledge of fraction representations differentiates middle school students with mathematics learning disability (dyscalculia) vs. low mathematics achievement. Journal of experimental child psychology, 115(2), 371-387. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2013.01.005
title: Use visual fraction models to support students with mathematics learning disability, but treat the transition from visual models to Arabic notation as a persistent obstacle
description: The article finds that visual fraction models lead to more accurate magnitude comparisons than Arabic numeral fractions for all ability groups, and that for children with MLD this visual model advantage persists through Grade 8. The authors state that "children in the MLD group may benefit from continued use of visual models as one of several a strategies to support learning about fractions and solving problems involving fractions". However, they caution that if children with MLD rely on models as concrete rather than abstract representations, visual models may not promote thorough conceptual understanding, especially when models are spatially misleading or when transitioning to Arabic notation.
requirements: Visual models should be used alongside other strategies, not as the sole representation
constraints: The article states visual models may not promote the intended conceptual understanding when they are spatially misleading or when transitioning from visual models to Arabic notation; for MLD children the visual model advantage persisted through Grade 8 rather than fading as it did for TA peers
target_learners: Middle school students with mathematics learning disability (dyscalculia)
target_learning_goals: Accurate magnitude comparison of fractions and conceptual understanding of fraction quantities
examples: In the study, accuracy was greatest when visual models involved matching parts and lowest with Arabic numbers, and the spatially misleading format continued to misguide students with MLD through middle school

article_title: Factors associated with acceptance of peers with mental health problems in childhood and adolescence
citation: Swords, L, Heary, C & Hennessy, E 2011, 'Factors associated with acceptance of peers with mental health problems in childhood and adolescence', Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry and Allied Disciplines, vol. 52, no. 9, pp. 933-941. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-7610.2010.02351.x
title: Vignette-based booklet measure of children's acceptance of hypothetical peers with ADHD and depression
description: A data-collection instrument in which participants completed a booklet of questions in response to two vignettes describing the behaviour of hypothetical target peers, one with depression and one with ADHD. It was administered to 595 participants drawn from five age groups spanning early childhood to late adolescence, sampled from schools randomly selected in the east of Ireland. The article describes it as "a booklet of questions in response to two vignettes describing the behaviour of hypothetical target peers with depression and ADHD."
requirements: Requires vignettes describing target peer behaviour and age-appropriate question booklets for each age group.
constraints: Measures responses to hypothetical peers rather than actual classmates.
target_learners: Children and adolescents across five age groups from early childhood to late adolescence
target_learning_goals: Assessing children's acceptance and perceptions of peers with mental health problems
examples: Administered to 595 participants in schools randomly selected in the east of Ireland.

article_title: Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency
citation: Zhou X, Wei W, Zhang Y, Cui J, and Chen C (2015) Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency. Front. Psychol. 6:1364. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01364
title: The visual perception hypothesis of the numerosity–arithmetic relation
description: The article proposes that a non-numerical factor—visual perception—accounts for the close relation between numerosity processing and mathematical performance because both tasks are typically based on rapid visual information processing. The authors state: "Here we propose that a non-numerical factor—visual perception—can account for the relation between numerosity processing and mathematical performance because both tasks are typically based on rapid visual information processing." This contrasts with the magnitude processing hypothesis and the inhibitory control hypothesis.
requirements: Both numerosity processing and arithmetic tasks must rely on rapid visual information processing for the hypothesis to explain their association
constraints: The hypothesis applies specifically to computational fluency rather than general mathematical achievement, and the speed of visual perception is critical
target_learning_goals: arithmetic computational fluency
key_sources: Zhou X, Wei W, Zhang Y, Cui J, and Chen C (2015) Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency. Front. Psychol. 6:1364. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01364

article_title: Parent, Teacher, and Student Perspectives on How Corrective Lenses Improve Child Wellbeing and School Function
citation: Dudovitz, R. N., Izadpanah, N., Chung, P. J., & Slusser, W. (2016). Parent, Teacher, and Student Perspectives on how Corrective Lenses Improve Child Wellbeing and School Function. Maternal and Child Health Journal. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10995-015-1882-z
title: Vision to Learn (VTL) school-based vision program
description: Vision to Learn is a non-profit, established in 2012, that partners with schools to provide free corrective lenses to low-income students. School nurses conduct screenings; a mobile eye clinic visits the school site, pediatric optometrists perform comprehensive exams after parental consent, students choose frames, and glasses are delivered to the school about two weeks later, with free replacement pairs. The program covers frames, lenses, exams, and administration at roughly $100 per child.
requirements: School nurse support to conduct the initial screening exam, which the article states is the only cost to schools
constraints: The article describes the program for low-income elementary school populations in Los Angeles
target_learners: low-income elementary school students with correctable visual deficits
target_learning_goals: improving access to and use of corrective lenses to support school function
examples: Three Los Angeles elementary schools (two public, one Catholic) serving predominantly Latino students participated in the evaluation

article_title: Enhanced verbal abilities in the congenitally blind
citation: Occelli Valeria, Lacey Simon, Stephens Careese, Merabet Lotfi B., Sathian K. (2017). Enhanced Verbal Abilities in The Congenitally Blind. Experimental Brain Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5436932/
title: Visual cortex involvement in language processing may underlie the verbal advantage in congenital blindness
description: The article proposes a neural account for the verbal advantage: visual cortical areas in congenitally blind people are recruited for language processing. The authors cite evidence that covert verb generation recruits early visual cortex, that visual cortical activity during word-list recall correlates with verbal memory performance, and that visual cortex shows stronger resting-state connectivity with language areas in the congenitally blind. This framework links cross-modal neuroplasticity to the behavioral verbal superiority observed in this study.
requirements: Requires congenital blindness, as the neural reorganization is attributed to the absence of vision from birth
constraints: The authors state the mechanism by which the superiority of verbal abilities occurs is currently unknown; this neural account is offered as a possibility
target_learning_goals: Understanding neural bases of verbal memory and language processing
examples: Covert verb generation in response to nouns presented via Braille or auditory input recruits activity in early visual cortex
key_sources: Occelli Valeria, Lacey Simon, Stephens Careese, Merabet Lotfi B., Sathian K. (2017). Enhanced Verbal Abilities in The Congenitally Blind. Experimental Brain Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5436932/

article_title: Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics
citation: Yang X and Meng X (2020) Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics. Front. Psychol. 11:462. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00462
title: Visual processing as a domain-general precursor of early academic learning
description: The article proposes that visual processing — the ability to attend to and distinguish a figure's features such as shape, orientation, color, and size — is a domain-general cognitive precursor supporting both character reading and early mathematics. It argues children must visually discriminate similar characters and mentally represent quantities and number relations, so the same basic visual skill organizes information across academic domains. The article concludes that "visual processing served as a domain-general indicator that contributed to organizing information to help solve diﬀerent types of academic problems, in spite of nonverbal intelligence, inhibitory control, and attention."
requirements: Visual processing must be measured independently of general cognitive abilities (nonverbal IQ, sustained attention, inhibitory control) to demonstrate its unique contribution
constraints: Evidence in this article is longitudinal-correlational; the authors state intervention studies are needed to investigate causality
The orientation discrimination task covers only one kind of visual discrimination (orientation), not shape, color, or size
target_learners: Mainland Chinese kindergarten children transitioning to grade one
target_learning_goals: Chinese character reading
early mathematics (calculation and word problems)
examples: The study measured visual processing with an orientation discrimination task and followed children from senior kindergarten to grade one

title: Visual-motor integration as the coordination of visual perception and motor coordination subcomponents
description: The article treats the visual-motor system as comprising two subcomponents — visual perception (processing ocularly obtained environmental information) and motor coordination (controlling fine and gross motor components of body movement) — whose fluid coordination is termed visual-motor integration. Deficits may arise in either subcomponent or in the integration of the two, and the article measures each separately with the Beery VMI subtests to determine which components predict which academic domains. constraints: The article notes deficits may stem from subcomponents, from integration, or from other neurological impairments limiting effective integration; the study was not powered to test mediation and could not examine ADHD diagnostic status as a moderator due to sample size

target_learning_goals: Reading achievement
Math achievement
Written language achievement
examples: The study administered the Beery VMI's Visual-Motor Integration, Visual Perception, and Motor Coordination subtests and regressed KTEA-3 reading, math, and written language composites on all three components

title: Substitute virtual for physical instructional materials without loss of learning when the instructional method is preserved
description: When teaching conceptual and procedural goals such as experimental design, computer-based materials that replicate the physical materials' content and allow learners the same design choices can replace physical manipulatives. target_learning_goals: designing unconfounded experiments (control of variables strategy)
examples: Ninety-two fourth- and fifth-graders were randomly assigned to learn CVS with real springs and weights or with mouse-clicked, video-depicted versions of the same springs and weights; all children then transferred to physical ramps a week later.

citation: Mikko Haavisto, Tomi Jaakkola. (2026). Fifth graders study videos faster than illustrated texts: Studying rate, review strategies, and learning implications. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09817-z
title: Use videos with hybrid learner control for primary school multimedia learning, particularly for slower readers
description: The article's results indicate that children tend to watch and review videos linearly at their designed rate and sequence, leading to faster studying, better learning outcomes, and lower cognitive load compared to illustrated texts. Because "the videos were especially beneficial for the slower readers", and linear studying helped novices avoid skipping important content or disrupting coherence, videos with hybrid learner control are recommended for primary school science learning. Learning time should be controlled and sufficient for an initial pass plus review, as in a school lesson context

title: Video-based student-profile diagnosis task with eye tracking (11-min geometry lesson, five marked students)
description: The study's core element is an 11-min video of an eighth-grade introductory geometry lesson from a German high school, containing a whole-class question-answer scene (bottom-up drivers assumed) and an individual seatwork scene (top-down drivers assumed). Five students marked with letters B, E, K, P, T each represented one empirically identified profile (strong, struggling, overestimating, underestimating, uninterested) from a latent profile analysis. examples: The underestimating student raised the hand twice and took notes; the struggling student never raised her hand and often rested her head on her hands.

article_title: The Effective Design of Tasks Involving Learning by Drawing: Current Trends and Methodological Progress in Research on Drawing to Learn
citation: Dechamps, T., & Skulmowski, A. (2025). The Effective Design of Tasks Involving Learning by Drawing: Current Trends and Methodological Progress in Research on Drawing to Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10026-2
title: Two-level classification of visualizations in drawing tasks: abstractness level and representational vs. relational drawing type
description: The review proposes describing visualizations in learning-by-drawing studies on two levels: the level of visual abstractness (concrete vs. abstract) and the drawing type, distinguishing "visualizations representing tangible real-world objects, labeled as representational images" from "non-tangible concepts or abstract relationships, labeled as relational images," following Hegarty (2011) and Skulmowski (2024). Complex drawings such as multiple representations or animations form an additional category. The authors apply these labels to both provided reference images and learner-generated drawings to make studies comparable.
requirements: Studies should classify both provided and learner-generated visualizations using a shared terminology so results can be compared.
constraints: The classification is proposed for learning-oriented drawing tasks and relies on the conceptual systems of Hegarty (2011), Quillin and Thomas (2015), and Skulmowski (2024).
target_learners: learners using drawing as a learning strategy across educational domains
target_learning_goals: designing and comparing drawing-to-learn tasks and their visualizations
examples: The review classifies Schwamborn et al.'s (2010) drawing prompt as predominantly abstract, and Bobek and Tversky's (2016) tire-pump drawings as combining representational and relational elements with predominantly concrete elements.

article_title: The “simple” view of learning from illustrated texts and videos
citation: Haavisto, M., Lepola, J., & Jaakkola, T. (2025). The “simple” view of learning from illustrated texts and videos. Learning and Instruction, 100, 102200. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102200
title: Incorporate videos into primary science instruction to support learners with weaker reading skills
description: The article concludes that videos are beneficial across reading skill levels and especially for weaker readers: among fifth and sixth graders, "children with weaker decoding skills remembered more of what they learned from videos, while the benefit was less for those with average decoding and almost nonexistent for those with high decoding." Videos were not harmful for any reader group and produced more equitable retention. Teachers can identify likely beneficiaries with common decoding tests.
requirements: Access to video materials with spoken audio and learner controls on classroom devices
Decoding tests are common and easy to implement, allowing teachers to identify students most likely to benefit from video-based learning
constraints: Findings are from primary school science learning; extension to other domains and younger students needs further research
The modality effect was weaker when material was available during testing than in retention-based studying
target_learners: Fifth and sixth grade primary school students across reading skill levels
target_learning_goals: Science topic learning: retrieval, transfer, and long-term retention of expository content
examples: In the within-subjects experiment, children studied climate change and balance in nature from videos and illustrated texts on iPads in authentic lessons, with delayed tests one week later

article_title: How to foster STEM learning during Covid-19 remote schooling: Combining virtual and video experiments
citation: Flegr, S., Kuhn, J., & Scheiter, K. (2023). How to foster STEM learning during Covid-19 remote schooling: Combining virtual and video experiments. Learning and Instruction, 86, 101778. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101778
title: Use virtual experiments, optionally combined with video experiments, for guided inquiry learning when hands-on experimentation is not possible
description: The article concludes that "virtual and video experiments can be recommended to teachers if hands-on experimentation is not possible". In its study, guided inquiry learning with these formats during Covid-19 remote schooling significantly fostered seventh-graders' conceptual understanding of converging lenses, with guidance embedded in worksheets and instructional videos. Because combinations and sequences conferred no advantage over the virtual experiment alone, the virtual experiment is the essential component, with the video experiment an optional enrichment.
requirements: Guidance must be embedded in the learning material, such as experimentation worksheets and instructional videos, since a teacher cannot provide just-in-time support during remote schooling
Students need access to the digital experiments and materials, which were provided via links and regular mail in the study
constraints: The study was conducted during Covid-19 remote schooling with seventh-graders learning individually at home on the topic of converging lenses, so scope is limited to that setting and topic
No hands-on control group in a traditional classroom could be included, so learning cannot be compared to traditional classroom experimentation
The video experiment lacks interactivity, as students are "in the role of an attentive observer without having any opportunity to actively manipulate variables"
target_learners: Seventh-grade secondary school students (Gymnasium, highest German track) learning individually at home during remote schooling
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding in physics, specifically geometrical optics and image formation by converging lenses
examples: 154 seventh-graders were randomly assigned within classes to video-virtual, virtual-video, or virtual-only conditions and worked through a guided inquiry unit on converging lenses entirely from home

article_title: Research versus Propaganda in Visual Education.
citation: Frank N. Freeman. (1922). Research Versus Propaganda in Visual Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XI, No. 5. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/5/
title: Visual materials' distinctive advantages: sensory appeal, spatial and mechanical relationships, temporal transformation, and diffusion of expert presentation
description: Freeman identifies the probable advantages of visual materials to set against their limitations. Pictures possess immediate sensory appeal and share with textbooks the advantage of diffusing expert examples of presentation. Visual devices are particularly suitable for representing spatial relations, mechanical construction and operation, and graphs for presenting comparisons and trends, while motion pictures can slow rapid motion or speed up very slow movements to render them perceptible.
requirements: Concrete materials should be employed only for meanings that can be conveyed through sensory channels, since language remains essential for abstract meanings
constraints: Freeman notes H. G. Wells emphasized the diffusion advantage in an exaggerated fashion
target_learning_goals: concrete, spatial, mechanical, and temporal understandings conveyable through sensory channels
examples: Freeman's examples: a clearer notion of a geographic region from a map, mechanical contrivances better shown than described, and graphs as an unrivalled method for certain relationships

article_title: Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning
citation: Yu, H., Miao, C., Leung, C. and White, T. J. (2017). Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0016-3
title: Virtual learning companions with human traits for large-scale interactive learning support
description: Virtual learning companions (VLCs) are AI software agents with human-like characteristics proposed to provide interactive learning experience at scale in MOOCs. The article describes a curious companion that monitors progress and "identiﬁes learning contents that can potentially arouse the learner 's curiosity"; a remembrance companion helping learners recall previously acquired knowledge through progressively more explicit hints; and Betty's Brain, a teachable companion based on learning-by-teaching theories. VLCs also generate behaviour data for learning skill analytics.
requirements: VLCs need to be equipped with human-like characteristics to provide believable interactions
VLCs need to be able to hold meaningful conversations to facilitate learning of complex topics
Informed consent mechanisms from learners are needed in MOOC platforms using VLCs
constraints: The article states VLCs are not yet ready for MOOCs: AI conversational interaction remains an open research challenge, and ethical issues must be carefully deliberated
Limiting what VLCs can do to comply with ethical guidelines may not prevent learners from gaming them
target_learning_goals: maintaining learner interest and curiosity, recalling related knowledge, and consolidating knowledge through teaching
examples: Jill Watson, an AI teaching assistant built on IBM Watson, answers students' questions in Georgia Tech's Knowledge Based Artificial Intelligence MOOC

title: Viacocrea prototype: multi-user collaborative platform structuring cocreative problem-solving in six phases with digital creative techniques
description: The Viacocrea prototype is a multi-user collaborative digital platform used to support small-group cocreative problem-solving in real classroom PBL. It offers "a multi-user collaborative platform, a graphic representation of cocreative phases, and creative techniques aimed at structuring, supporting, enriching, and orchestrating small group cocreative problem-solving endeavours". In this study, five groups of secondary students followed six Viacocrea phases (Starting up, Defining, Designing, Building Up, Concluding, Communicating), performing two digital creative techniques per phase. The Learning Chain and Telescope techniques provided the idea dataset evaluated for novelty.
requirements: Groups work within a shared multi-user collaborative digital space in which all small-group members can annotate ideas
Teacher-selected creative techniques per phase to structure the cocreative process
constraints: The study reports no interaction between groups, only within each group

target_learning_goals: Collaborative creativity and cocreative problem-solving of open-ended scientific challenges
examples: Five groups of students in Lleida, Spain, each dedicated 18 hours to a cocreative inquiry on reducing Segre River pollution using the Viacocrea application

article_title: An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips
citation: Noemi Mauro, Liliana Ardissono, Federica Cena, Livio Scarpinati, Gianluca Torta. (2024). An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34, 793–824. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00366-x
title: Visual feasibility annotation of options against the itinerary's time constraints
description: This lesson/task-level design pattern keeps the planner constantly aware of the temporal feasibility of each candidate item while an itinerary is built incrementally. Each PoI and activity is annotated with "a green or red semaphore depending on whether the item can be included in the itinerary without exceeding the available time or not", alongside a continuously updated display of spare time. If the user disregards the indication and causes a scheduling error, the application explains the problem. In the study's thematic analysis, most participants considered awareness of the remaining time very useful, and some missed this functionality in the baseline planner.
requirements: An itinerary generator invoked after each item addition or removal so the next feasibility estimate relies on a refreshed, optimized schedule
constraints: The heuristic feasibility estimation may generate false negatives because it does not optimize the schedule of the revised itinerary and may overestimate displacement time
target_learners: Teachers planning multi-stop itineraries under fixed time budgets
target_learning_goals: Informed selection of places and activities that fit the trip's temporal constraints
examples: The interface shows spare time (e.g., 2 hours and 20 minutes) in the left section and per-item visit and setup times (e.g., 30 minutes execution + 10 minutes setup) next to each semaphore

title: Use videos and instructor feedback within online argumentation to support argument construction

Specific and direct feedback regarding what to write or change in arguments

article_title: Rubric formats for the formative assessment of oral presentation skills acquisition in secondary education
citation: Rob J. Nadolski, Hans G. K. Hummel, Ellen Rusman, Kevin Ackermans. (2021). Rubric formats for the formative assessment of oral presentation skills acquisition in secondary education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10030-7
title: Viewbrics online tool integrating video-modelling examples with analytic text-based rubrics and a progress dashboard
description: The Viewbrics tool is a dedicated online tool supporting formative assessment of oral presentation skills with analytic rubrics in text-based and video-enhanced versions. Video-modelling examples "contain question prompts that illustrate behavior associated with (sub)skills performance levels in context, and are presented by young actors the target group can identify with". It supports teacher, peer, and self-assessment, reflection, goal-setting, and a dashboard visualizing per-subskill progress (green improving, blue constant, red declining) with emoticon feedback. Its rubrics cover eleven subskills scored on four-point scales, organized under logos, ethos, and pathos.

Rubrics must be tailored to the specific learning objectives and target groups

Developing video-enhanced rubrics is more costly than text-based rubrics

citation: Friday Joseph Agbo, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Markku Tukiainen. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking. Education Tech Research Dev 71:505–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10161-5

As printed, "When students learn CT concepts through a theoretical approach, they can gain abstract knowledge that may not enhance their comprehension, hence a visualized approach to teaching CT concepts could be helpful to students." constraints: The study addresses abstract CT concepts (e.g., recursion) that students find difficult to comprehend through mathematical functions alone

examples: The Tower of Hanoi mini game was integrated to facilitate CT skills through visualization of recursion while experiencing gameplay in VR

Coach roles of coordinator, facilitator, and curator
Materials including priming tools, examples of practice, and artifacts of practice

article_title: The impact of visual aid displays showing a manipulative task
citation: Lasser, S. (1954). The Impact of Visual Aid Displays Showing a Manipulative Task. The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 6: Part 3, 95-106.
title: Lasser's account: visual-aid presentations are not stored as memory-images and do not furnish ready-made meanings

constraints: The account is theorized from the subjects' comments, not directly tested in the experiment.

article_title: Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study
citation: Romero-Zaldivar, V.-A., Pardo, A., Burgos, D., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2012). Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1058–1067. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.003
title: Virtual appliances as self-contained, instrumentable environments for learning analytics
description: The approach packages a course's full tool set in a virtual machine distributed to students, exploiting virtualization's isolation, compatibility and encapsulation so that "a multi-level comprehensive monitoring scheme can be deployed" inside the appliance. Rather than forcing activities onto a generic platform, the design places "generic 'sensors' closer to the environment in which students interact" — instrumenting applications with wrapper programs and relaying events through the Subversion client to a central server. target_learning_goals: predicting academic achievement
instructor monitoring and adjustment of course activities
examples: A second-year engineering course appliance configured with compiler, debugger, memory profiler, editor, browser and command interpreter, with events relayed via a Subversion wrapper

article_title: Relationships between critical thinking dispositions and evaluation of videos with variation in the level of expertise of the source among middle and high school students

title: Four fictitious interview videos and adapted French critical thinking disposition scales for adolescents
description: The study material comprises four 45–55-second fictitious interview videos on meat consumption reduction, in which the interviewee's position and expertise (expert vs layperson) varied, with expertise signaled by a banner and interview location. A trainer providing specific feedback about performance and suggestions for improvement

communication self-efficacy

Theoretical learning outcomes in vocational subjects

article_title: Virtual or blended laboratories for healthcare students education: a systematized review.
citation: Safaeipour Ruhollah, Aalaa Maryam, Mojtahedzadeh Rita, Mohammadi Aeen, Asadzandi Shadi, Mousavi Atekeh. (2025). Virtual or blended laboratories for healthcare students education: a systematized review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07937-7
title: Virtual laboratory as an online simulation tool applying real-world phenomena in a virtual space
description: The review defines a virtual laboratory as "an online simulation tool based on interactive learning that applies real-world phenomena in a virtual space," relying on Internet technologies so the platform is "accessible to students at any time and from anywhere." It distinguishes virtual laboratories (software-based simulation without real physical equipment) from remote laboratories (distance control of real equipment) and simulated laboratories (a broader category), preserving original terminology where studies used terms interchangeably.
requirements: Internet technologies to create an online environment accessible to students at any time and from anywhere
constraints: Terminology was occasionally used interchangeably across studies; the review preserved the original terminology used by the study authors

citation: Robbrecht M, Van Winckel M, Mulder A, Embo M. (2025). What is the learning effect of video review in postgraduate medical education: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06515-7
title: Video review should be integrated with feedback or coaching sessions rather than used in isolation
description: The review found that video review in PGME is typically implemented alongside structured feedback or coaching: "Most studies combined video review with feedback sessions or coaching [10, 29–31, 33, 35, 36, 38]". Transcript evidence from Mazer et al. suggests complementarity, with factual topics discussed intraoperatively and clinical reasoning predominating in video review sessions with supervisors. This supports designing video review as part of a blended learning arrangement rather than a standalone method.
requirements: Access to video recording equipment in clinical settings where cameras are not routinely used
Supervisor or coach availability for review sessions
constraints: Combining video with other interventions complicates assessment of video's isolated impact, per the review's own discussion
target_learning_goals: clinical skills
clinical reasoning
communication skills
examples: Mazer et al. demonstrated that discussion of anatomy and procedure steps occurred more intraoperatively while intraoperative decision making was discussed more during video-based coaching

article_title: Video Killed the Radio Star-A Meta-Analysis on Video-Based Coaching to Improve Surgical Skill.
citation: Anderson Steven Mark, Gillanders Sarahlouise, Hickey Anne, Offiah Gozie, Davis Niall. (2025). Video Killed the Radio Star—A Meta‐Analysis on Video‐Based Coaching to Improve Surgical Skill. World Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1002/wjs.12494
title: Video-based coaching as a mechanism for reproducing the trainee–trainer feedback relationship outside the operating room
description: Video-based coaching (VBC) is a training method in which "a coach provides individualized feedback on a trainee's performance after reviewing video footage of their performance together". The article positions VBC as reproducing the conventional trainee–trainer relationship of the apprenticeship model without the time constraints of the operating room and without the need for sophisticated simulation models. In the review, VBC sessions involved trainees watching video of their own performance with expert feedback, varying in session count, length and timing across the included RCTs.
requirements: Video footage of the trainee's performance and a coach able to review it with the trainee and deliver individualized feedback
constraints: All included studies scored a high risk of performance bias because it is not possible to blind participants or personnel to VBC or control
target_learning_goals: surgical technical skill acquisition
examples: In the included RCTs, coaching sessions ranged from a single session to 10, lasted 10 to 45 min, and occurred from immediately following the procedure to 2 weeks after it; 14 studies used one-to-one review of the video with a coach

procedural skills
knowledge
attitudes
satisfaction

constraints: No procedure-related errors to patients, per the review's stated advantage over bedside teaching

Endoscopic manual skills acquisition

article_title: How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review.
citation: Whiting Penny F, Davenport Clare, Jameson Catherine, Burke Margaret, Sterne Jonathan A C, Hyde Chris, Ben-Shlomo Yoav. (2015). How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4521525/
title: Use visual aids alongside frequency or probability formats to further improve post-test probability estimation
description: The review reports that visual aids to present information, applied to both probabilities and natural frequencies, further improved health professionals' post-test probability estimation beyond format effects alone. One RCT found natural frequencies with graphical aids produced the highest proportion of correct estimates at 73%, compared with 68% for probabilities with graphical aids, 48% for natural frequencies alone and 23% for probabilities alone. The authors recommend visual presentation as a means of facilitating improved understanding of diagnostic information.
requirements: Graphical displays must be designed to correspond with the accuracy information being presented, such as probability modifying plots or circle graphics
constraints: The review states this finding was based on a single study, limiting generalisability
target_learners: health professionals including doctors and other clinicians
target_learning_goals: estimating post-test probability of disease
interpreting diagnostic test results
examples: One RCT compared natural frequencies and probabilities each with and without graphical aids, finding the combined format produced the highest proportion of correct estimates

description: Virtual Walking the Pens is a serious digital game designed to assist swine producers in learning production and management practices through digital gaming. Students interact with a simulated virtual swine confinement operation, performing virtual barn walkthroughs in which they identify and treat unhealthy pigs; "the game allowed students to experience 10 swine disease scenarios within a virtual world". Basic workplace mathematical problems using addition, subtraction, fractions, ratios, and percentages were embedded in each scenario, such as completing a veterinarian report.
requirements: Teachers received training on the game from technical and pedagogical perspectives, and completed weekly online fidelity reports during the 10-day treatment
constraints: The study used the game for only 10 consecutive instructional days, which the authors note limits conclusions about longer-term effects
target_learners: secondary agricultural education students in animal science courses
target_learning_goals: swine health and management knowledge
basic workplace mathematics skills
examples: Treatment teachers' students played the game for 10 consecutive instructional days after teachers attended a two-day professional development session at Oklahoma State University

developing positive attitudes towards environmental issues

target_learning_goals: geometry concepts in the Nigerian senior secondary mathematics curriculum

citation: Maher, C. A., Palius, M. F., Maher, J. A., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Sigley, R. (2014). Teachers Can Learn to Attend to Students' Reasoning Using Videos as a Tool. Issues in Teacher Education, 23(1). https://www.videomosaic.org
title: Video Mosaic Collaborative (VMC): a searchable online database of videos, tasks, and resources of students engaged in mathematical problem solving
description: The Video Mosaic Collaborative is a searchable database built from a quarter-century of research on mathematical reasoning, making "videos, tasks, and related resources available via the Internet (www.videomosaic.org)". Its videos feature the same students followed over time solving cognitively challenging tasks, with multiple cameras capturing talk and inscriptions, and a researcher facilitating small-group and whole-class discourse. The counting-combinatorics strand videos were used in the teacher-education interventions reported here, and the resources are openly accessible for courses and professional development.
requirements: Videos were produced through long-term research that followed the same students over time, with well-documented examples of reasoning identified by many scholars
constraints: The assessment video was used only for assessment purposes and not by any MTEs in designing an intervention
target_learners: pre-service and in-service K-12 mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: recognizing and describing students' mathematical reasoning and arguments
examples: Experimental participants worked on counting tasks, watched VMC videos of children solving the same problems, and discussed variations among teacher and student solutions

article_title: Teachers Can Learn to Attend to Students' Reasoning Using Videos as a Tool
citation: Maher, C. A., Palius, M. F., Maher, J. A., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Sigley, R. (2014). Teachers Can Learn to Attend to Students' Reasoning Using Videos as a Tool. Issues in Teacher Education, 23(1). https://www.videomosaic.org
title: Video as a pedagogical tool providing a virtual entry into classrooms and opportunities for analytic thinking unavailable in live observation
description: The article grounds its work in a framework assuming people learn best when actively engaged in interpreting the world, with video providing "a bridge that connects prior learning to new knowledge". Because video is "not live," it enables one to rewind, re-watch, review, and reflect, providing teachers opportunities for analytic thinking that live classroom observations or clinical interviews cannot. Video offers a shared focal representation for professional development and lets teachers discern what is important and compare with their own lived experiences.
requirements: A facilitated learning context in which teachers study videos of student reasoning
constraints: The framework addresses teacher recognition of student reasoning; transfer to live classroom practice remains a conjecture for future research
target_learning_goals: building knowledge about students' mathematical reasoning
attending to student reasoning in live classrooms
examples: The interventions used videos from prior long-term research showing students making sense of problems and persevering in solving them

article_title: The Effect of Virtual vs. Traditional Classroom Instruction on Creative Thinking of Iranian High School EFL Learners
citation: Soheila Shafiee Varzaneh & Roya Baharlooie. (2015). The Effect of Virtual vs. Traditional Classroom Instruction on Creative Thinking of Iranian High School EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n5p177
title: Design learning environments that leverage virtual instruction to foster learner creativity
description: The article's findings serve "as guidelines for designing classroom environments that can improve the creativity of learners." Because VLI produced significantly larger creative thinking gains and more positive attitudes than traditional instruction, the authors recommend integrating virtual learning environments when the goal includes fostering creativity, particularly for lower-proficiency learners who showed the largest gains.
requirements: Instruction must be mediated appropriately, as the article notes appropriate mediation helps improve learning and increase creative thinking
constraints: Evidence comes from one study of female Iranian high school EFL learners in a single course
target_learning_goals: creative thinking
positive attitudes toward learning
examples: The VLI group used a weblog system over 14 sessions while the TCI group learned the same material in a traditional classroom

article_title: Effectiveness of Video Podcast in Learning Psychology among Bachelor of Education Students
citation: K. Thiyagu. (2014). Effectiveness of Video Podcast in Learning Psychology among Bachelor of Education Students. i-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1078764
title: Use video podcasts to support learning of conceptually dense theoretical content
description: The study recommends video podcasting as an instructional technique for content-heavy theoretical subjects. The authors state that "educators could adapt the technique vodcasting for Instructing Educational Psychology, since vodcasting technique helps the teacher trainees to retain their attention during instruction." Videos were developed from prescribed syllabus topics, validated by experts, and shared via URL for self-paced learning.
requirements: Videos must be developed from prescribed syllabus content and validated by a panel of experts for content and presentation quality
constraints: The advantage did not extend to application-level objectives in this study
target_learning_goals: Educational Psychology learning theories content
examples: Four learning theories topics (Trial and Error, Classical Conditioning, Operant Conditioning, Insight Learning) were developed into video podcasts and shared with students via website URLs

citation: K. Thiyagu. (2014). Effectiveness of Video Podcast in Learning Psychology among Bachelor of Education Students. i-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1078764
title: Video Podcast on Educational Psychology learning theories for B.Ed trainees
description: A video podcast instructional resource covering four learning theories topics from the B.Ed Educational Psychology syllabus: Trial and Error, Classical Conditioning, Operant Conditioning, and Insight Learning. target_learning_goals: Understanding learning theories in Educational Psychology

article_title: Classmate Peer-Coaching: "A Study Buddy Support Scheme"
citation: Thalluri, Jyothi; O'Flaherty, Jackie A.; and Shepherd, Paul L. (2014). Classmate peer-coaching: "A Study Buddy Support scheme". Journal of Peer Learning, 7, 92-104. http://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol7/iss1/8
title: Virtual classroom delivery of the SBS scheme for external students
description: The virtual classroom (VC) is a tool for delivering live synchronous e-learning that mimics the face-to-face classroom and delivers content live over the Internet to geographically dispersed students, making it suited to external HB1 students. Staff trained Buddies and Leaders before commencing, sessions were recorded so external students could access them at their own time and pace, and content coverage and session numbers were identical for internal and external groups.
requirements: Key staff conduct VC training sessions for Buddies and Buddy Leaders before commencing
The course coordinator sets up the classroom weekly, converting materials to suitable formats such as PDFs and multiple-choice polls
constraints: Because internal and external students' results were combined, the article states it is difficult to comment on what the data say specifically about the virtual classroom
target_learners: external (off-campus) first-year Nursing students studying Human Body 1
target_learning_goals: synchronous peer support and real-time interaction for geographically dispersed students
reduced anxieties of isolation and disconnectedness
examples: An external student commented that the VC "allowed us to ask questions in real time and interact with others and the tutor."

article_title: The Effect of Video-Based Tasks in Listening Comprehension of Iranian Pre-Intermediate EFL Learners
citation: Abdullah Sarani, Esmail Zare Behtash and Saieed Moslemi Nezhad Arani. (2014). The Effect of Video-Based Tasks in Listening Comprehension of Iranian Pre-intermediate EFL Learners. Gist Education and Learning Research Journal, No. 8, pp. 29-47. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/1692-5777
title: Use video rather than audio-only materials for listening instruction because visual cues convey contextual and paralinguistic meaning
description: The article argues that video shows speakers, background situational cues, paralinguistic features, and non-verbal communication, so "an important part of the overall message is conveyed by the visual image." Audio-only scripts must be more verbally explicit to compensate for missing visual cues, which the article says leaves students ill-prepared for real-life, less explicit interaction. Video's technical features (freeze frame, review, preview) also give teachers control to facilitate comprehension.
requirements: Well-designed video-based activities; the article warns that authenticity alone does not transfer to real life where learners must also initiate language
constraints: The article notes video can distract listeners and cannot avoid ambiguity of interpretation, citing Aulia (2005)
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension of authentic spoken language
examples: The experimental group's materials were standard English video clips (Top Notch TV programs) with video-based tasks, while the control group used the same objectives via audio only

article_title: The Effect of Expansion of Vision Span on Reading Speed: A Case Study of EFL Major Students at King Khalid University
citation: Basim Hamdan Ibrahim Kana'an, Salahud Din Abdul Rab & Ahlullah Siddiqui. (2014). The Effect of Expansion of Vision Span on Reading Speed: A Case Study of EFL Major Students at King Khalid University. English Language Teaching, 7(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n10p57
title: Vision expansion drills A to N adapted from Cutler's Triple Your Reading Speed
description: A set of training drills used as the study's intervention instrument: "Vision expansion drills (Drills A to N) adopted from Triple Your Reading Speed by Cutler (1993, pp. 47-71)". The drills train learners to take in groups of words per eye fixation rather than reading letter-by-letter, and the test group received training sessions with them. The appendix illustrates a Two Stop Method drill focusing on the third word from the beginning and before the end of every line.
requirements: Training sessions extended to learners over the study period, with pre- and post-testing on matched texts of approximately equal length (740 and 710 words) and two sets of 10 comprehension questions
constraints: The study applied the drills to a small group of 50 final-year EFL undergraduates with above intermediate proficiency in the Saudi EFL context
target_learning_goals: increase reading speed in English as a foreign language
maintain reading comprehension while reading faster
examples: The test group received the drills as training sessions; the control group received none, and both groups were tested for speed and comprehension before and after training

article_title: Between-Case Standardized Mean Differences: Flexible Methods for Single-Case Designs
citation: Man Chen, James E. Pustejovsky, David A. Klingbeil, and Ethan R. Van Norman. (2023). Between-Case Standardized Mean Differences: Flexible Methods for Single-Case Designs. Journal of School Psychology, vol. 98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2023.02.002
title: Guide single-case effect size model specification with visual analysis and preliminary model-comparison analyses, and report sensitivity analyses across plausible specifications
description: The article recommends that analysts choose the hierarchical model for single-case data by first using visual inspection of the data series, then conducting preliminary analyses such as information criteria and likelihood ratio tests. It states: "we recommend researchers using visual analysis to guide the initial model specification and then conduct preliminary analyses, including information criteria and likelihood ratio tests, to reach an appropriate model specification." Because different specifications yield different effect size estimates, it also recommends reporting sensitivity analyses across plausible models.
requirements: Researchers should use theory and disciplinary knowledge to guide model specification
Preliminary analyses such as visual inspection of predicted values, likelihood ratio tests, or AIC/BIC comparisons
constraints: Different model specifications lead to different effect size estimates, so the choice must be justified and checked for sensitivity
target_learners: school psychologists and education researchers analyzing single-case design data
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation and reporting of design-comparable effect sizes from single-case studies
examples: For the Thiemann and Goldstein (2001) data, visual inspection showing stable baseline and treatment phases led to a model without time trends; for the Bryant et al. (2018) data, visual inspection and preliminary analyses supported a model with linear time trends in each phase

article_title: Inculcating Positive Thinking in the Self-Concept of Children with Learning Difficulties
citation: Mohaned Ghazi Abed. (2016). Inculcating Positive Thinking in the Self-Concept of Children with Learning Difficulties. i-manager's Journal on Educational Psychology, Vol. 10, No. 3. https://www.imanagerpublications.com
title: Values in Action (VIA) Inventory of Character Strengths Survey for youth
description: The VIA Inventory is Peterson and Seligman's device for defining and categorizing character strengths and virtues, adapted for youth as the VIA Strengths Survey for Young People. In this study it was completed by each child with learning difficulties to establish individual strengths, and was combined with three class lectures on positive psychology as the intervention. The article notes that "adults on a global scale endorsed 24 character strengths" in prior international trials, and that positive psychology studies had not yet been adapted for children with LD.
requirements: Completion by each child to identify his individual character strengths as the basis of the strength-focused intervention
constraints: The article notes a need for a larger sample to facilitate in-depth analysis of the VIA Survey's reliability and validity
target_learners: children with learning difficulties aged 12–14 in intermediate schools
target_learning_goals: identifying personal character strengths
improving self-concept
examples: The VIA Survey was administered together with three class lectures on positive psychology over a five-week intervention course in Jeddah schools

article_title: The Effect of Virtual versus Traditional Learning in Achieving Competency-Based Skills
citation: Mosalanejad, L.; Shahsavari, S.; Sobhanian, S.; & Dastpak, M. (2012). The effect of virtual versus traditional learning in achieving competency-based skills. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 13(2). https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tojde
title: Virtual simulation and interactive multimedia program for the Nursing Fundamentals and Skills course
description: An internet-based instructional arrangement in which theoretical subjects were taught "by using digital systems (digital libraries) and virtual animations" and practical procedures were taught with video systems and virtual animations, followed by lab practice with instructor analysis of skill difficulties. It was evaluated against conventional face-to-face teaching and moulage demonstration in a quasi-experimental study of 86 nursing students, with the final theoretical exam and OSCE held constant across groups.
requirements: Access to digital libraries, virtual animations and video systems, plus lab practice sessions with an instructor reviewing skill difficulties
constraints: Evaluated in one course (3 theoretical and 1 practical credits) at a single medical sciences university with matched but non-randomized groups
target_learning_goals: competency-based theoretical knowledge and practical clinical skills
examples: The same instructor taught both groups; the virtual group practiced in the lab after video and animation demonstration and had skill difficulties analyzed by the instructor
