article_title: The Effect of Second Life on Speaking Achievement
citation: Guzel, S. & Aydin, S. (2016). The effect of second life on speaking achievement. Global Journal of Foreign Language Teaching. 6(4), 236-245. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1100452
title: Use virtual worlds like Second Life as a complement to traditional speaking instruction
description: Because SL practice produced significant speaking gains and descriptively larger improvements than traditional sessions, the article supports integrating virtual worlds into speaking classes. The authors conclude that "SL's contribution to speaking performance surpasses that which traditional speaking sessions have accomplished," while also noting both environments positively influence achievement. Educators can therefore adopt SL-based speaking activities as a beneficial supplement or alternative to classroom-only instruction.
requirements: Access to the SL platform, structured lesson plans, and assessment instruments such as the Kanatlar (2005) Speaking Grading Scale.
constraints: Between-group post-test differences were not statistically significant, so the advantage of SL over traditional instruction is descriptive rather than confirmed statistically.
target_learning_goals: Speaking achievement including grammar, vocabulary, intelligibility, fluency, and task achievement
examples: Third-year EFL learners completed four weekly 45-minute speaking sessions in SL using an advanced-level course book.

article_title: Supporting Student Veterans: Utilizing Game-Based Role-Plays with Virtual Humans to Build Military Cultural Competency and Helping Behaviors in Faculty and Staff
citation: Cate, C. A., & Albright, G. (2015). Supporting Student Veterans: Utilizing Game-Based Role-Plays with Virtual Humans to Build Military Cultural Competency and Helping Behaviors in Faculty and Staff. Online Learning, 19(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1074245
title: Use game-based virtual-human role-plays with ongoing feedback to train faculty and staff in gatekeeper and cultural competency skills.
description: The article supports using online role-play simulations with emotionally responsive virtual humans to train gatekeepers, because "the majority of gatekeeper training programs do not employ active-learning strategies such as role rehearsal." Virtual humans adapt their behaviors to learners' conversation tactics and react verbally and nonverbally, providing immediate feedback. The authors argue this model offers advantages over face-to-face training, including reduced social evaluative threat, sustainability, and high training fidelity through standardization.
requirements: The simulation must provide realistic role-plays with continual feedback in a safe and confidential learner environment, standardized to each participant every time.
constraints: Follow-up scores declined from posttraining levels, implying it would be useful to have refresher training at periodic intervals.
target_learning_goals: build gatekeeper skills to support students in psychological distress
build military cultural competency
examples: Participants role-played with three emotionally responsive virtual student veterans, practicing motivational interviewing tactics such as asking open-ended questions and reflective listening.

article_title: From Memorising to Visualising: The Effect of Using Visualisation Strategies to Improve Students' Spelling Skills
citation: Nahari, A. A., & Alfadda, H. A. (2016). From Memorising to Visualising: The Effect of Using Visualisation Strategies to Improve Students' Spelling Skills. English Language Teaching, 9(6), 1. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n6p1
title: Spelling instruction should move beyond phonetic memorisation toward visual memory strategies for irregular orthographies.
description: Because English spelling does not follow a close relationship between phonemes and graphemes, the article argues that "all words cannot be correctly spelled according to how they sound but they can be spelled correctly according to how they look". Teachers should therefore emphasise visual memory and mental imagery as core spelling strategies, especially for learners whose first language has a more phonetic script.
requirements: Teachers must recognise and articulate the various strategies a speller can use when required to spell an unfamiliar word
constraints: No single technique can cover all aspects of teaching and learning spelling or suit all language students with their diverse needs
target_learners: Students whose first language has a phonetic orthography
target_learning_goals: Correct English spelling
Reduced spelling anxiety and frustration
examples: The study trained students to visualise word images rather than rely on phonetic patterns, resulting in significant spelling gains
key_sources: Nahari, A. A., & Alfadda, H. A. (2016). From Memorising to Visualising: The Effect of Using Visualisation Strategies to Improve Students' Spelling Skills. English Language Teaching, 9(6), 1. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n6p1

article_title: From Memorising to Visualising: The Effect of Using Visualisation Strategies to Improve Students' Spelling Skills
citation: Nahari, A. A., & Alfadda, H. A. (2016). From Memorising to Visualising: The Effect of Using Visualisation Strategies to Improve Students' Spelling Skills. English Language Teaching, 9(6), 1. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n6p1
title: Visual memory for word images as a mechanism underlying successful spelling.
description: The article proposes that spelling is fundamentally a visual process: good spellers access a visual memory of a word's appearance, check it kinaesthetically, and verify it looks right. This mechanism, drawing on NLP-based accounts (Blackerby, 2001; Hamilton, 2000) and Bell's Seeing Stars premise, explains why visualisation strategies outperform purely phonetic approaches for words with irregular spellings.
requirements: Learners must have encountered the target word previously to form a visual memory of it
constraints: The mechanism is described for English, an opaque orthography; applicability to transparent orthographies is not addressed
target_learning_goals: English spelling accuracy
Recognition and correction of misspelled words
examples: Good spellers' eyes move up-left to access visual memory, then down to check accuracy kinaesthetically, before looking up again to verify the word looks right

article_title: Promoting Student Teachers' Content Related Knowledge in Teaching Systems Thinking: Measuring Effects of an Intervention through Evaluating a Videotaped Lesson
citation: Rosenkränzer, F., Kramer, T., Hörsch, C., Schuler, S., & Rieß, W. (2016). Promoting Student Teachers' Content Related Knowledge in Teaching Systems Thinking: Measuring Effects of an Intervention through Evaluating a Videotaped Lesson. Higher Education Studies, 6(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v6n4p156
title: Video-based measurement instrument: videotaped lake-ecosystem lesson with six planted CK and PCK mistakes and an analysis booklet
description: To measure reflective CRK in a situational context, the authors developed "a video with an associated booklet" showing a lesson in which 6th graders learn about the ecosystem lake. The authors "installed six mistakes in the video vignette, three in each form of CRK", such as an incorrect definition of a system and a confusing map of labeled interactions. Student teachers analyzed the video and noted erroneous situations; notes were coded (0-6 score) with Krippendorff's alpha over .80. Expert review led to omitting multiple-choice options to avoid anticipations.
requirements: Expert validation of the vignette's critical aspects
trained coders and a coding scheme (Mayring, 2007) for scoring notes
constraints: Due to the limited number of items, Cronbach's alpha was not meaningful; reliability was supported by test-retest correlation (r=.583**) and convergent validity correlations
target_learners: student teachers at universities of education
target_learning_goals: reflective professional knowledge (CK and PCK) for teaching systems thinking
examples: The video was used at all three measurement points (pretest, posttest, follow-up) to capture reflective CRK

article_title: Effect of Video-Cases on the Acquisition of Situated Knowledge of Teachers
citation: Geerts, W. M., Steenbeek, H. W., & van Geert, P. L. C. (2018). Effect of Video-Cases on the Acquisition of Situated Knowledge of Teachers. International Education Studies, 11(1), 64. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n1p64
title: Use video cases in teacher education to promote the development of situated knowledge through targeted application.
description: The article recommends targeted use of video cases in teacher education because they contain explicit details of recorded situations presented contextually and holistically, allow trainees to apply theoretical knowledge by analyzing authentic educational situations, and do not contain textual interpretation that steers the reader. Video cases are particularly well-suited to have trainees analyze scenes, make educational purposes their own, and apply design patterns as situated knowledge.
requirements: Higher order learning objectives requiring analyzing, evaluating or creating study materials
constraints: Teacher trainers focus insufficiently on higher learning objectives when using video cases
target_learners: Pre-service teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: Development of situated knowledge, design patterns, and educational purposes
examples: The experimental course used video cases from the Didiclass database, including the 'Olga' case illustrating all components of the design pattern 'Dealing with disorder'.

article_title: Impact of e-AV Biology Website for Learning about Renewable Energy
citation: Nugraini, S. H., Choo, K. A., Hin, H. S., & Hoon, T. S. (2013). Impact of e-AV Biology Website for Learning About Renewable Energy. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1070414
title: Use video-based e-learning websites to make abstract biology processes comprehensible and engaging
description: The article recommends using multimedia websites that integrate video, animation, and textual information to teach abstract or complex biology processes that are difficult to explain in the classroom, such as biofuel production. Video lessons allow students to visualise processes that are otherwise hard to observe, while the website format supports independent, individual learning. The authors found this approach improved both knowledge and interest compared with conventional teaching.
requirements: Computer laboratory and Internet access for students to use the website individually
constraints: The study was conducted only in International schools in one major Indonesian city over a short time frame
target_learners: Senior high school students in Indonesia
target_learning_goals: Understanding abstract biotechnology and renewable energy processes
examples: Students viewed videos such as 'Video of Renewable Energy on Biosolar' and 'Video of Renewable Energy of Jatropa Oil Production' individually through the website.
key_sources: Nugraini, S. H., Choo, K. A., Hin, H. S., & Hoon, T. S. (2013). Impact of e-AV Biology Website for Learning About Renewable Energy. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1015407

title: Virtual museums should be integrated into history teaching to enhance motivation and conceptual understanding.
description: The article concludes that virtual museums can enhance students' motivation and conceptual understanding in history education. Based on the significant attitude improvement and positive student feedback, the author recommends that "These kinds of activities should be applied in the schools" and that schools be equipped with the necessary technology.
requirements: Schools should be equipped with computer and internet technologies for virtual museum applications.
Students should have sufficient prior knowledge about the subjects.
constraints: Virtual museums lack detailed object information, audio features, and bird's-eye views, which students found limiting.

increase motivation and conceptual understanding in history
examples: The study used five Turkish virtual museums, including the Anıtkabir Virtual Museum and 360-degree panoramic tours of the Ankara Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, over a two-month implementation period.

citation: Ulusoy, K. (2010). Open Education Students' Perspectives on Using Virtual Museums Application in Teaching History Subjects. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 11(4). https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tojde/issue/16922/176560

description: Virtual museums are web-based collections of digitized artefacts, images, and information that students can explore remotely. constraints: Cannot fully replace the experience of original objects; lacks detailed object information, audio features, and bird's-eye views.

develop understanding of cultural heritage
